newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers seek fees in Texaco race case.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers seek fees in Texaco race case.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
Plaintiffs lawyers in a widely watched racial discrimination case against Texaco Inc. on Tuesday requested payment of 25 percent of the cash part of the record settlement to be paid to claimants.

Daniel Berger, a New York lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said the amount would actually come to about 17 percent of the $176.1 million settlement after plaintiffs receive salary increases retroactive to January 1997 and other provisions of the plan take effect.
The request for legal fees came as part of a fairness hearing on the proposed settlement, the biggest in a discrimination case in the United States.
There were no objections to the proposal from the crowd that packed the hearing in White Plains, N.Y., federal court and U.S. District Judge Charles Brieant took the settlement under advisement.

Berger said the fee was reasonable considering the "excellence" of the outcome and the risk to the lawyers who took the case on a contingency fee basis. Discrimination cases are very difficult to win and just one year before the pending suit was filed, a federal judge denied class certification in a sex discrimination suit against Texaco.
"This was a very risky proposition for counsel," Berger said. Berger is with the New York law firm of Bernstein Litowitz Berger & Grossman.
Michael Hausfeld of Washington-based Cohen, Milstein, Hausfeld & Toll, another plaintiffs' firm, said that under the accord, plaintiffs will receive awards ranging from $60,000 to $80,000.

He described the settlement as "one of the most publicly scrutinized," yet one that produced a "rare consensus" between the parties. Notices were sent to more than 1,300 potential plaintiffs but none chose to opt out of the accord.

The case received widespread attention after transcripts of tape recordings submitted as evidence in the proceedings showed executives allegedly discussing the destruction of documents and making racist remarks.

Although Texaco denies fault, it agreed on Nov. 15 to pay $176.1 million to settle the 1994 class action lawsuit filed by black employees who alleged they were discriminated against in pay and promotions.
As part of the settlement, Texaco developed a plan to boost employment, career development and recruiting of minorities, as well as increasing purchasing from minority- and women-owned companies.
The class included all blacks employed in salaried positions at Texaco or its subsidiaries at any time from March 23, 1991, through Nov. 15, 1996.
The plan was well received by civil rights groups and by the Rev. Jesse Jackson, who responded by calling for an end to a consumer boycott of Texaco he helped initiate in November.
Texaco also reached an agreement with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission so that the agency can intervene in the settlement.
Under the accord, the EEOC will have certain rights to receive information, monitor the settlement and participate in court proceedings.

Texaco fired a top executive of an insurance subsidiary and took actions against other current and former employees who can be heard on the tapes. The moves came after the company received a final report from an outside lawyer who investigated the situation.

The tapes were made public after Richard Lundwall, former senior coordinator of personnel services of Texaco's finance department, turned them over to the plaintiffs lawyers in the discrimination case. He and other executives can be heard on the tapes planning to destroy documents requested by the plaintiffs.
Although Lundwall turned over the tapes, he was indicted last week for obstruction of justice. He is the only defendant facing criminal charges growing out of the discrimination case.
Texaco's stock fell 75 cents to $101 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
